key_insight: Rarefied hypersonic surface loads over triangular protrusions have different nonlocal support lengths, with heat transfer showing the strongest bulk-to-wall dependence, pressure being moderately nonlocal, and shear remaining hardest to identify.
engineering_relevance: Designers of hypersonic vehicles may need different sensing or surrogate-fidelity ranges for heat transfer, pressure, and shear because one radius does not capture all wall-load physics.
method: DSMC simulations over Mach 4–8, Kn 0.1–0.8, and three protrusion orientations
Region-to-point diagnostics using circular neighborhoods with weighted statistics, extrema, nearest-point values, and tangent-normal gradients
Compare full-domain vs truncated radii using errors in Cp, Cq, and |tau|, and test ridge-regression/threshold surrogate controls
evidence_signal: Full-domain descriptors reduced error from 45.5% to 13.8% for Cp and from 72.6% to 12.9% for Cq, while shear improved only from 49.1% to 31.9%, with R95 defined from 5% error convergence.
watch_item: The inferred support length depends on the chosen neighborhood summary and surrogate setup, so the partial preservation observed in closed-loop tests may not transfer unchanged to other geometries or flow regimes.
paper_title: Quantity-Dependent Bulk-to-Wall Observability of Surface Loading in Rarefied Hypersonic Flow over Triangular Protrusions
